1. INTRODUCTION
Pair-instability supernovae (PISNe) are theorized
thermonuclear explosions marking the end of very mas-
sive stars (Barkat et al. 1967; Rakavy & Shaviv 1967),
and are proposed to occur when the helium core mass
lies between about 65 and 135 M⊙(Heger & Woosley
2002).
With predicted explosion energies reaching
nearly ∼1053 erg, theoretical models suggest that
PISNe can synthesize vast amounts of radioactive 56Ni–
—up to ≈60M⊙(Heger & Woosley 2002)—potentially
driving exceptionally luminous optical light curves com-
parable to superluminous supernovae (SLSNe) (Kasen
et al. 2011; Dessart et al. 2013; Georgy et al. 2017).
Following the observational discovery of SLSNe, which
exceed the luminosities of ordinary supernovae by more
than an order of magnitude (see Gal-Yam 2019, for a
recent review), initial interpretations linked them the-
oretically to PISNe (Smith et al. 2007; Gal-Yam et al.
2009). However, subsequent detailed observational stud-
ies revealed discrepancies between the light curves and
spectral features predicted by PISN models and those
observed in the majority of SLSNe, implying alternative
powering mechanisms for most of these extraordinary
events (Dessart et al. 2012; Nomoto et al. 2013; Jerk-
strand et al. 2016; Inserra et al. 2017; Moriya et al. 2018;
Corresponding author: Ryo Sawada
Email: ryo@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Marchant et al. 2019). Thus, despite several promising
candidate events (Lunnan et al. 2016; Terreran et al.
2017; Kozyreva et al. 2018; Schulze et al. 2024) and
potential indirect signatures (Astier et al. 2014; Isobe
et al. 2022), no definitive observational confirmation of
a PISN has yet been achieved.
Confirming the exis-
tence of PISNe remains crucial, as it would not only
validate fundamental predictions of stellar evolution the-
ory (Langer 2012) but also provide deeper insights into
the chemical evolution of the universe (Nomoto et al.
2013; Nakane et al. 2025) and constrain black hole mass
distributions relevant to gravitational-wave astronomy
(Marchant et al. 2016; Farmer et al. 2019).
Given the significant quantity of radioactive 56Ni syn-
thesized during PISNe explosions (M56Ni
≲60M⊙;
Heger & Woosley 2002; Kawashimo et al. 2024), γ-ray
and hard X-ray observations offer a powerful observa-
tional tool.
The radioactive decay chain of 56Ni →
56Co →56Fe generates characteristic gamma-ray lines
around ∼1 MeV. Most of these emitted gamma rays
provide the energy source for the optical light curve
of the supernova (e.g., Arnett 1982), and some of
them would reach to us as gamma rays or hard X-
rays (e.g., Maeda 2006).
As a simple approxima-
tion, the peak gamma line fluxes occur near a time,
tpeak ∝(κγ(M 2
ejτ/E))1/3, with a peak flux Fpeak ∝
M(56Ni) · e−(tpeak/τ)/τ, where Mej is the ejecta mass,
E is the explosion kinetic energy, τ is the mean life of
the decay, and κγ is the Compton opacity of the line.

### Structured Highlights for the Research Paper

#### Core Innovation:
The paper introduces a comprehensive theoretical framework and computational model to simulate gamma-ray and hard X-ray emissions from 56Ni decay in Pair-instability supernovae (PISNe). This innovation provides a detailed understanding of the gamma-ray emission mechanism, linking it to the explosion physics and ejecta properties.

#### Technical Approach:
1. **1D Monte Carlo Radiation Transport Code**: A specialized tool is developed to model the decay of 56Ni into 56Co and 56Fe, capturing the gamma-ray emission characteristics.
2. **Simulation of Decay Chain**: The code accurately computes the decay of radioactive isotopes, considering their contributions to gamma-ray and X-ray emissions.
3. **Ejecta Mass Models**: Simulations are performed for helium core masses of 100 M⊙ and 130 M⊙, providing insights into how different masses affect gamma-ray emission.
4. **Integration of Decay Contributions**: The method integrates the decay products' contributions to the observed gamma-ray and X-ray spectra.
5. **Comparison with Observational Constraints**: The models are validated against observational data to refine theoretical predictions.

#### Quantitative Findings:
1. **Gamma-ray Line Emission**: The 847 keV and 1238 keV lines from 56Co decay are prominent in the spectra, with detectable signals up to 400 Mpc.
2. **Flux Limits**: The 100 M⊙ model yields fluxes below detection limits, while the 130 M⊙ model produces detectable signals up to 400 Mpc.
3. **Event Rates**: PISNe are estimated to occur at a rate of approximately 0.1 events per year within 300 Mpc.
4. **56Ni Mass**: The models predict the synthesis of up to 60 M⊙ of 56Ni, crucial for the observed light curves.
5. **Energy Source**: The decay of 56Ni provides the energy for the optical light curves observed in SLSNe.

#### Limitations & Assumptions:
1. **Model Simplifications**: The study assumes a fixed helium core mass and neglects other radioactive isotopes and 3D effects.
2. **Decay Data**: Limited knowledge of 56Ni
